blocks.text:
Java 8 was released in March 2014 and it is still the most common version you will meet in old enterprise code. Java 25, the current long-term-support (LTS) release, came out in September 2025. In between lie seventeen releases and a very different language. If you read a tutorial from 2015 and a codebase from 2025 side by side, they look like two dialects. This chapter is your map: what arrived when, which features change how you write everyday code, and which ones you can safely ignore for now.

The reason to know this is practical. In an interview you will be asked "what is new since Java 8?". At work you will inherit a project on Java 11 or 17 and have to decide what you may use. And when you read someone else's code you need to recognise `record`, `sealed`, `case Point(int x, int y)` and `var` on sight.

### How releases work

Since Java 10 a new feature release appears every six months, in March and September. Every second year one of them is designated LTS: 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25. Vendors support LTS releases for years, while the releases in between get about six months of updates. Production systems usually sit on an LTS and move from one to the next; the non-LTS versions are where new features first appear in final form.

Features do not appear fully formed. A new language or library feature usually goes through **preview** (shipped but switched off unless you pass `--enable-preview`, and allowed to change) and sometimes **incubator** (a separate module whose API may change), before it becomes final. A feature that has been "preview" for several releases is not unstable junk; it is being refined with feedback. The unit of change is the **JEP** (JDK Enhancement Proposal), a numbered document at `openjdk.org/jeps/<number>`; when you want the real story of a feature, search for its JEP.

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `sealed` plus `switch` gives you a compiler-checked "this covers every case". Add a third `Shape` and `area` stops compiling until you handle it. That is the single biggest win of modern Java for domain modelling.
- `case null` is allowed in a pattern switch. Before Java 21 a `switch` on a null reference threw `NullPointerException` unconditionally.
- `reversed()` returns a view, not a copy. Sequenced collections (Java 21) add `getFirst`, `getLast`, `addFirst`, `reversed` to `List`, `Deque`, `LinkedHashSet` and friends so you no longer write `list.get(list.size() - 1)`.

### What to adopt and what to ignore

Not every new feature deserves equal attention. A sensible ranking for a backend developer:

rows: Use for locals when the right-hand side makes the type obvious (`var users =` `new ArrayList<User>()`). Avoid when it hides the type (`var x = compute()`).
Adopt for DTOs, value objects, map keys, multiple return values. Not for JPA entities (they need mutable state and a no-arg constructor).
Adopt for SQL, JSON, HTML snippets in code.
Adopt. They replace most old `switch` statements and cannot fall through.
Adopt for closed hierarchies: results, events, commands, AST nodes.
Prefer over `collect(Collectors.toList())` when you do not need a mutable result.
Adopt for blocking server-style code on Java 21+; not a speed-up for CPU-bound work.
Use the new methods when the code is on 21+.
Use instead of `HttpURLConnection` for new code.
Know how they work; most applications still run on the classpath.
Learn them, but do not ship them. They require `--enable-preview` and a matching JDK.
blocks.caption: Adoption guide.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Check which Java your project targets before using a feature. In Maven this is `maven.compiler.release`; in Gradle it is the toolchain. Using `--release 17` makes `javac` reject Java 21 APIs, not only syntax. That protects you from calling `List.reversed()` in code that must run on 17.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What has changed in Java since version 8 that you actually use? Name a handful and say why, not just what: `var` for less noise; records for immutable data carriers; sealed interfaces with pattern `switch` for exhaustive handling of a closed set of cases; text blocks for multi-line strings; `Optional` and streams (Java 8) with `Stream.toList()`; virtual threads in 21 for cheap blocking concurrency; and the new six-month release cadence with LTS every two years. Mention that you target an LTS and that preview features need `--enable-preview`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Java has a feature release every March and September; LTS releases are 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25.
- Features move through preview or incubator stages before they are final; read the JEP for the real story.
- Highest value since 8: `var`, records, text blocks, switch expressions, sealed types, pattern matching, virtual threads, sequenced collections.
- Target an LTS and pin the language level with `--release`; do not ship preview features.

Compiling with `javac` by hand works for one file. A real project has hundreds of source files, tests, and dozens of third-party libraries, each with its own dependencies. A **build tool** automates the repeatable parts: download the right library versions, compile, run tests, package the result, and do it the same way on your laptop and on the build server. In the Java world the two dominant tools are **Maven** and **Gradle**. Spring Boot projects use either; Maven is more common in enterprises, Gradle in Android and many newer projects.

blocks.text:
### Maven: convention over configuration

Maven's central idea is that if every project uses the same directory layout and the same sequence of steps, you can describe a project with a short declarative file, the **POM** (`pom.xml`), instead of a script. The standard layout is:

blocks.code:
project/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/java/com/example/lib/App.java       production code
    ├── main/resources/application.properties    files copied to the jar
    └── test/java/com/example/lib/AppTest.java   test code

blocks.text: A minimal POM looks like this. The three values `groupId`, `artifactId` and `version` (the **GAV coordinates**) identify the project, and any library, uniquely.

blocks.code:
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>lib</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
      <version>5.11.0</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</project>
blocks.title: pom.xml

blocks.text:
The version shown is only an example; look up the current release on Maven Central (`search.maven.org`) before you copy it.

#### The build lifecycle

Maven has built-in **lifecycles** made of ordered **phases**. You ask for a phase and Maven runs every earlier phase first. The default lifecycle phases you use daily:

rows: compile and run unit tests (Surefire plugin)
copy the artifact to your local repository `~/.m2`
upload the artifact to a remote repository
blocks.caption: Main phases of the default lifecycle, in order.

blocks.text: Two more lifecycles exist: `clean` (deletes `target/`) and `site`. So `mvn clean package` means "delete old output, then run everything up to and including `package`". Each phase is just a set of **plugin goals** bound to it: `compile` runs `compiler:compile`, `test` runs `surefire:test`. When you need extra behaviour, such as building an executable Spring Boot jar, you add a plugin to the POM.

blocks.text: On this book's build machine Maven 3.9 is installed but the sandbox cannot reach Maven Central, so the commands below were not run here. The output you see on your own machine begins with `[INFO] Scanning for projects...` and ends with `BUILD SUCCESS`.

blocks.code:
$ mvn -v
$ mvn clean package
$ mvn test
$ mvn -q -DskipTests package
$ mvn dependency:tree
$ mvn -pl service -am package
blocks.title: Everyday Maven commands

blocks.text:
`dependency:tree` is the command you will use most when debugging. It prints what Maven resolved, including the transitive (indirect) dependencies. `-pl service -am` builds only the `service` module and the modules it depends on ("also make").

### Dependencies, scopes and conflicts

A dependency is another jar identified by GAV. Maven downloads it from a **repository** (by default **Maven Central**) into a local cache (`~/.m2/repository`) and also downloads that library's own dependencies. These indirect ones are **transitive dependencies**.

The `scope` says when a dependency is on the classpath:

rows: default; available everywhere and passed on to consumers
needed to compile, supplied by the runtime (for example the servlet API in a server)
not needed to compile, needed to run (for example a JDBC driver)
only in `dependencyManagement`, to import a bill of materials (BOM)
blocks.caption: Dependency scopes.

blocks.text: When two paths pull in different versions of the same library, Maven applies **nearest wins**: the version closest to your project in the dependency tree is used (first declaration wins on a tie). This can silently choose an old version. The fix is explicit: declare the version you want in `dependencyManagement`, or exclude the unwanted transitive dependency. A **BOM** (bill of materials), such as Spring Boot's, is a POM that lists compatible versions of many libraries so you do not set each one.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: `SNAPSHOT` versions (`1.2.0-SNAPSHOT`) mean "work in progress" and can change under you. Never depend on a SNAPSHOT in a release. Pin versions in release builds so the same commit produces the same result next month.

### Gradle: the same job as a script

Gradle uses a build script rather than XML. It is more flexible and, with its build cache and daemon, often faster on big projects; the price is that a script is code and so easier to make hard to read. The equivalent of the POM above, in the Groovy-based `build.gradle`:

blocks.title: build.gradle

blocks.text:
Gradle's configurations map roughly to Maven scopes: `implementation` (compile, not exposed to consumers), `api` (exposed; from the `java-library` plugin), `runtimeOnly`, `compileOnly` (provided) and `testImplementation`. Tasks replace phases: `./gradlew build`, `./gradlew test`, `./gradlew run`, `./gradlew dependencies`. Newer projects often use the Kotlin DSL (`build.gradle.kts`) with the same structure.

#### The wrapper

Both tools offer a **wrapper**: small scripts (`mvnw`, `gradlew`) committed to the repository that download the exact tool version the project wants. Anyone who clones the repo runs `./mvnw package` or `./gradlew build` and needs no pre-installed Maven or Gradle, only a JDK. This removes "works with my Maven 3.6" problems and is what CI servers should call. Always commit the wrapper files.

### Multi-module projects and repositories

Large applications split into modules, each with its own POM, under a parent POM that lists them and shares versions:

blocks.code:
<packaging>pom</packaging>
<modules>
  <module>domain</module>
  <module>service</module>
  <module>web</module>
</modules>
blocks.title: parent pom.xml (fragment)

blocks.text: `service` declares a dependency on `domain` like on any other artifact; Maven builds the modules in dependency order. Gradle expresses the same with `settings.gradle`: `include 'domain', 'service', 'web'`. Do not confuse these build modules with Java modules (`module-info.java`) from Part 10; build modules are a grouping for compilation, Java modules are a runtime and compile-time visibility mechanism. Repositories come in three kinds: **local** (`~/.m2`, your cache), **remote** (Maven Central or a company server), and a **repository manager** such as Nexus or Artifactory that proxies Central for the whole company and stores private artifacts. `mvn deploy` publishes to the last kind.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In a Spring Boot service the POM usually has `spring-boot-starter-parent` as its parent (it supplies a BOM and plugin configuration). A dependency like `spring-boot-starter-web` is a "starter": one line that pulls in a consistent set of libraries. Understanding scopes and `dependency:tree` is how you diagnose the classic "NoSuchMethodError at runtime" caused by two versions of one library.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between Maven and Gradle, and what does `mvn install` do? Maven is declarative XML with a fixed lifecycle and strong conventions; Gradle is a script (Groovy or Kotlin) with a task graph, incremental builds and a build cache, so it is more flexible and often faster. `mvn install` runs all phases up to `install`, which copies the built artifact into the local repository `~/.m2` so other local projects can depend on it. `deploy` is the phase that publishes to a remote repository.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A build tool resolves dependencies, compiles, tests and packages repeatably.
- Maven: `pom.xml`, standard layout, GAV coordinates, lifecycle phases run in order up to the one you ask for.
- Scopes control when a dependency is on the classpath; transitive conflicts resolve to the nearest version, so inspect with `dependency:tree`.
- Gradle uses a script and tasks; both tools provide a wrapper that you should commit.
- Pin versions and avoid SNAPSHOTs in releases.

A test is a small program that runs your code and fails loudly when the result is not what you expected. Without tests every change is a gamble: you fix one bug, you break another, and you find out in production. With a good test suite you can refactor, upgrade Java or replace a library and know within minutes whether behaviour changed. For a job interview, "how do you test your code?" is asked almost as often as "how does HashMap work?".

### The test pyramid

Tests differ in scope, and scope decides speed and reliability.

blocks.code:
/\
     /  \        few   end-to-end / UI tests     slow, brittle, realistic
    /----\
   /      \      some  integration tests         real DB, real HTTP, a Spring context
  /--------\
 /          \    many  unit tests                one class, no I/O, milliseconds
/------------\

blocks.text:
A **unit test** exercises one class or method in isolation, runs in milliseconds, and needs no network, database or clock. An **integration test** wires several parts together (your repository class with a real database such as one started in a container). An **end-to-end test** drives the whole system from the outside. The pyramid advice is: write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few end-to-end tests, because the higher you go, the slower the feedback and the more often tests fail for reasons that are not bugs.

### What makes a test good

- **Fast and deterministic.** The same input gives the same result every time. A test that depends on the current time, random numbers or thread timing is a flaky test; inject a `java.time.Clock` or a seeded `Random` instead.
- **Independent.** A test must not depend on another test having run first. Each test builds its own objects.
- **Tests one behaviour** and is named after it: `depositRejectsNegativeAmount`, not `test1`.
- **Arrange, Act, Assert.** Set up the objects, call the code, check the outcome. Three visible parts.
- **Fails for one reason**, with a message that tells you what was expected and what happened.
- **Tests behaviour, not implementation.** If a harmless refactoring breaks twenty tests, they were too tightly coupled to private details.

### JUnit 5

**JUnit 5** is the standard test framework. It is built from three parts: the *Platform* (launches tests; IDEs and Maven/Gradle talk to it), *Jupiter* (the API you write tests against) and *Vintage* (runs old JUnit 3/4 tests). Add `org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter` with `test` scope and your tests live under `src/test/java`. The listing below is shown as text because the sandbox cannot download JUnit; the next section runs a hand-made equivalent so you can see the mechanism.

blocks.title: AccountTest.java (needs JUnit 5 on the classpath; not run here)

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- **Lifecycle.** `@BeforeEach` and `@AfterEach` run around every test; `@BeforeAll` and `@AfterAll` run once per class (they must be `static` unless you change the instance lifecycle). JUnit creates a *new instance of the test class for each* *test method*, which is why fields set in one test do not leak into another.
- **Assertions.** `assertEquals(expected, actual)`: expected first. Swapping them gives a confusing failure message. `assertThrows` returns the exception so you can inspect it. `assertAll` reports every failing check instead of stopping at the first.
- **Parameterized tests** run one method with many inputs: `@ValueSource` for simple values, `@CsvSource` for rows of arguments, `@MethodSource` for arbitrary objects.
- Test methods and classes can be package-private; they do not need to be `public`. `@Disabled` skips a test; `@Nested` groups tests inside an inner class.

You run them with `mvn test` or `./gradlew test`; both print a summary such as `Tests run: 4, Failures: 0`.

### A tiny test runner you can run now

To see there is no magic, here is a 60-line framework with a `@Test` annotation, a fresh instance per test, two assertions and a pass/fail report. It uses reflection (covered in Part 10) to find annotated methods, which is essentially what JUnit's engine does, plus a lot of polish. Run it with `java MiniTest.java`.

blocks.title: MiniTest.java

blocks.code:
$ java MiniTest.java
PASS depositIncreasesBalance
PASS depositRejectsZero
FAIL deliberatelyBroken -> expected <1> but was <0>
2 passed, 1 failed
blocks.title: Typical output (the method order from reflection is not guaranteed)

blocks.text:
Notice the last line: the runner exits with a non-zero status when any test fails. That is how a build server knows to stop the pipeline, and it is exactly what Surefire does for `mvn test`. Also notice that `getDeclaredMethods()` does not promise an order; JUnit likewise says test order is deliberately not obvious, so never rely on it.

### Making code testable: inject the clock

The most common reason code is hard to test is that it reaches out to something global: the system clock, a random generator, a static singleton. The cure is to pass the dependency in. For time, `java.time.Clock` is built for this: production code receives `Clock.systemUTC()`, tests receive a fixed clock.

blocks.title: Cl.java

blocks.code:
$ java Cl.java
false true
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
Both boundary cases, the last day and the first day after, are now exact and repeatable, something a test using `LocalDate.now()` could only pass on one particular day. The same trick applies to `Random` (pass a seeded instance), to `UUID` generation (pass a `Supplier<UUID>`) and to file access (pass a `Path`, and use a temporary directory in the test). Constructor injection is nothing more than that: dependencies arrive as parameters. This is also what Spring does for you, and it is why well-designed Spring code is easy to test without Spring at all.

### Mocks and fluent assertions

Real classes have collaborators: a service calls a repository, which calls a database. To unit-test the service alone you replace the repository with a **test double**. **Mockito** is the common library for generating one:

blocks.title: OrderServiceTest.java (needs Mockito; not run here)

blocks.text:
The idea is *stubbing* (`when(...).thenReturn(...)` decides what the double answers) and *verification* (`verify(...)` asserts it was called). Use mocks for slow or non-deterministic collaborators (database, HTTP, clock). Do not mock simple value objects, and do not verify every call: a test that mirrors the implementation line by line breaks on every refactoring. Where you can, prefer a small **fake** (an in-memory repository) to a mock; it keeps the test about behaviour.

**AssertJ** replaces JUnit's `assertEquals` with readable, chainable assertions that give better failure messages: `assertThat(names).containsExactly("Asha", "Ravi").doesNotContain("Zed");`. It is a taste, not a necessity.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring Boot, `spring-boot-starter-test` bundles JUnit 5, Mockito and AssertJ. `@SpringBootTest` starts the whole application context (an integration test, slow); `@WebMvcTest` loads only the web layer; plain unit tests with no Spring annotation are fastest. Teams that see 10-minute builds usually have too many `@SpringBootTest` tests where a unit test would do. For database tests, Testcontainers starts a real database in Docker, which is more faithful than an in-memory substitute.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A test that passes is not proof that the code is right: coverage tools measure which lines ran, not whether you asserted anything. A test with no assertion, or one that catches and swallows the exception, can reach 100% line coverage and verify nothing. Mutation testing and code review are the antidotes.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you decide what to test, and what is the difference between a mock and a stub? Test behaviour that matters through public methods: normal cases, boundaries (0, 1, empty, maximum), and failure paths (invalid input, exceptions). A stub supplies canned answers to the code under test; a mock additionally records calls so that the test can verify an interaction happened. Prefer state-based assertions on results; verify interactions only when the interaction itself is the requirement (for example "an email was sent").

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Follow the pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few end-to-end tests.
- Good tests are fast, deterministic, independent, focused on one behaviour and named for it.
- JUnit 5: `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `assertEquals(expected, actual)`, `assertThrows`; a fresh instance per test.
- Use doubles (Mockito or hand-written fakes) for slow collaborators; do not over-verify interactions.
- Coverage numbers do not prove correctness.

Writing code is half of the job; the other half is getting it onto a server and running it reliably. This chapter follows an application from compiled classes to a runnable artifact, to a trimmed runtime, to a native installer, and finally to a container. Each step answers the question "what does the person running this need to have installed?"

### Jars

A **JAR** (Java ARchive) is a zip file of class files, resources and a `META-INF/MANIFEST.MF`. It is how libraries are distributed and, with a `Main-Class` entry in the manifest, how simple applications are run. Create one with the `jar` tool:

blocks.title: com/example/Greeter.java

blocks.code:
$ javac -d out com/example/Greeter.java
$ jar --create --file greeter.jar --main-class com.example.Greeter -C out .
$ java -jar greeter.jar Maruthi
Hello Maruthi
$ unzip -p greeter.jar META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
Manifest-Version: 1.0
Created-By: 21.0.12.1 (Ubuntu)
Main-Class: com.example.Greeter
blocks.title: Build and run an executable jar

blocks.text: `--main-class` writes the `Main-Class` line, so `java -jar` knows where to start. `-C out .` means "change into `out` and add everything". If your program needs libraries, a plain jar does not contain them: you need `-cp app.jar:lib/*` (on Windows `;`), or a **fat jar** (also called uber jar) that bundles the dependencies. Spring Boot builds an executable fat jar with its Maven or Gradle plugin and a custom class loader that reads the nested jars. The `maven-shade-plugin` and the Gradle `shadow` plugin are the generic alternatives.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: `java -jar` ignores any `-cp` you pass; the jar's manifest `Class-Path` entry decides. This surprises people who try to add a driver jar on the command line.

### jlink: a runtime made for your application

Normally a user needs a whole JDK or JRE installed. The module system (Part 10) lets you ship only the parts of the JDK your program uses. `jdeps` finds which modules a jar needs, and `jlink` builds a custom runtime image containing just those.

blocks.code:
$ jdeps --print-module-deps --ignore-missing-deps greeter.jar
java.base
$ jlink --add-modules java.base --output rt --strip-debug --no-header-files \
    --no-man-pages --compress zip-6
$ rt/bin/java --list-modules
java.base@21.0.12.1
$ rt/bin/java -jar greeter.jar Asha
Hello Asha
$ du -sh rt /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64
39M     rt
286M    /usr/lib/jvm/java-21-openjdk-amd64
blocks.title: jdeps and jlink

blocks.text:
The custom runtime is 39 MB against 286 MB for the full JDK on this build machine (sizes depend on platform and vendor). A real application adds modules such as `java.sql` or `java.net.http`. `jlink` needs your dependencies to be modular or automatic modules; with big classpath applications (Spring Boot) it is awkward, and teams more often use the full JRE in a container image instead.

### jpackage: a native installer

`jpackage` takes your application and a runtime and produces a platform installer: `.msi` or `.exe` on Windows, `.dmg` or `.pkg` on macOS, `.deb` or `.rpm` on Linux. It is for desktop applications, not servers. A typical call:

blocks.code:
jpackage --name Greeter --input target --main-jar greeter.jar \
         --main-class com.example.Greeter --type deb

blocks.text:
It must be run on the operating system you are targeting (no cross-building) and needs platform packaging tools. It bundles a jlink-style runtime, so the installed application needs no separate Java. The tool is installed here (`jpackage` `--version` prints 21.0.12.1), but producing a package requires the OS tooling, so the command above was not run.

### Java in containers

Most backend Java now runs in Docker or Kubernetes. A container image holds a JRE, your jar and a start command. A typical `Dockerfile` uses a **multi-stage build**: compile with a full JDK, then copy only the jar into a small runtime image.

blocks.code:
# Stage 1: build
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package

# Stage 2: run
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar app.jar
RUN useradd --system appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-jar", "app.jar"]
blocks.title: Dockerfile (not run here: no Docker daemon in the build sandbox)

blocks.text:
Notes on this file: the second stage contains only a JRE and the jar, so the image is far smaller and has fewer tools for an attacker; running as a non-root user is a basic security habit; `ENTRYPOINT` in exec form (a JSON array) makes `java` process number 1, so it receives `SIGTERM` when the container stops and shutdown hooks run. Image tags such as `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` select a vendor distribution; pin a specific tag in production.

#### Memory inside a container

The JVM is **container aware** (since Java 10, backported to 8u191): it reads the cgroup memory limit and CPU quota rather than the host's totals. By default the maximum heap is 25% of the container memory (`MaxRAMPercentage=25`). That default is conservative because the process also needs memory outside the heap: Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and the GC's own structures. You can see the flag logic on any machine:

blocks.title: Heap sizing flags (this build machine's container limit is about 6 GB; typical values)

blocks.text: Practical rules: prefer percentages (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70` or 75) over a fixed `-Xmx`, so the same image works with different container sizes; leave 25-30% headroom for non-heap memory, otherwise the kernel's OOM killer ends the container (exit code 137) while the Java heap looks fine; and set a CPU limit knowing that it changes how many processors the JVM sees, which sizes the GC and `ForkJoinPool` thread counts. A container with less than two CPUs or about 1.8 GB of memory is treated as a "small" machine and, before Java 27, selects the Serial collector instead of G1; the last chapter of this Part explains the change in Java 27.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: A container with a memory limit of 512 MB and `-Xmx512m` will be killed. The limit covers the whole process, not just the heap. Start from `MaxRAMPercentage` of 50-75 and watch real usage with `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory` (needs `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`).

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Boot can build an image without a Dockerfile (`./mvnw spring-boot:build-image`) using Cloud Native Buildpacks, which also calculate sensible memory settings. Startup time matters for autoscaling; techniques to cut it (class-data sharing, AOT caches, GraalVM native image) are the subject of the next chapters.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Your Java service keeps being killed in Kubernetes with exit code 137, but heap dumps show the heap is fine. What is going on? Exit 137 means the process received `SIGKILL`, usually from the OOM killer, because total process memory exceeded the container limit. The heap is only part of the memory: Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers and the code cache count too. Reduce `MaxRAMPercentage`, cap thread counts and direct memory, and measure with Native Memory Tracking.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- A jar is a zip of classes plus a manifest; `java -jar` needs `Main-Class`, and dependencies need a classpath or a fat jar.
- `jdeps` plus `jlink` produce a small custom runtime; `jpackage` builds native installers for desktop apps.
- Containers: multi-stage build, JRE-only final image, non-root user, exec-form `ENTRYPOINT`.
- The JVM reads container limits; heap defaults to 25% of memory, so tune `MaxRAMPercentage` and leave room for non-heap memory.
- Exit code 137 usually means the OOM killer, not a Java `OutOfMemoryError`.

Java 25 is the LTS release that most teams will move to from Java 17 or 21 over the next two years, so it is worth understanding what it actually changes. Think of it in three groups: features that make **small programs and learning** **easier** (compact source files, instance `main`, module imports), features that make **code safer and cleaner** (flexible constructor bodies, scoped values), and features that make the **JVM leaner and faster to start** (compact object headers, AOT ergonomics).

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: The sandbox that built this book has only JDK 21. Listings marked "Java 25; not run on 21" are checked against the JEP text (openjdk.org/jeps) but were not executed. Where a Java 21 preview gives a runnable cousin of the feature, that is shown and labelled. Verify new listings on a JDK 25 before relying on them.

### Compact source files and instance main (JEP 512)

Every Java tutorial starts with a ceremony that students cannot yet explain: `public class`, `public static void` `main(String[] args)`, `System.out.println`. JEP 512 (final in Java 25, the result of previews in 21 to 24) removes the ceremony for small programs without creating a second language.

The rules:

- A **compact source file** may contain top-level methods and fields. The compiler wraps them in an implicitly declared class (final, in the unnamed package, named after the file, and not referable from other code).
- The `main` method no longer has to be `public static void main(String[] args)`. The launcher looks, in order, for a `static main(String[])`, a `static main()`, an instance `main(String[])`, then an instance `main()`. For an instance method it creates an object using a non-private no-argument constructor.
- Compact source files automatically `import module java.base`, so `List`, `Map`, `Stream` and `Path` need no imports.
- `java.lang.IO` has `IO.println`, `IO.print`, `IO.readln` for simple console input and output, without `System.out` or `Scanner`.

blocks.title: Hi.java (Java 25; not run on 21)

blocks.text: On Java 25 you run it with `java Hi.java`. On Java 21 the closest thing is the preview of the same idea (JEP 445), which does need `--enable-preview`, and where `System.out.println` is still required. This is real output from the build machine:

blocks.title: Hi.java (Java 21 preview version; this was run)

blocks.code:
$ java --enable-preview --source 21 Hi.java
Note: Hi.java uses preview features of Java SE 21.
Note: Recompile with -Xlint:preview for details.
Hello, compact source file
42
blocks.title: Terminal
Note
blocks.text: A compact source file is a convenience for scripts, exercises and learning. A growing program is meant to graduate: add a `class` declaration and the file becomes an ordinary one. Real services keep using normal classes, and frameworks such as Spring Boot do not care about any of this.

### Module import declarations (JEP 511)

Imports are usually a source of noise: a dozen `import java.util.*` style lines. `import module java.base;` imports, on demand, every public top-level class and interface of every package that the module `java.base` exports. So `List`, `Map`, `Stream`, `Path`, `BigDecimal` all become available at once.

**Report.java (Java 25; not run on 21)**

Two things to know. First, if two imported modules export a class with the same simple name (the classic is `java.util.Date` against `java.sql.Date` after `import module java.sql;`), a use of the simple name is ambiguous and does not compile; a single-type import such as `import java.util.Date;` resolves it. Second, the feature changes the source only, not the program's runtime dependencies: the code still needs the module to be present. Many style guides will probably still prefer explicit imports in long-lived code, so treat module imports as a tool for scripts and teaching, which is what the JEP targets.

### Flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513)

Java has always required `super(...)` or `this(...)` to be the first statement of a constructor. That forced awkward code: to validate an argument before calling the superclass constructor you had to hide the check inside a static helper called from the argument expression. JEP 513 (final in 25) allows statements **before** the explicit constructor call, as long as they do not touch the object that is still being built.

The constructor body is now conceptually two parts: the **prologue** (before `super(...)`) and the **epilogue** (after). In the prologue you may validate arguments, compute values to pass up, and assign fields declared in the same class (only fields without an initializer); you may not read `this`, call instance methods, or use `super.something`.

blocks.title: Employee.java (Java 25; not run on 21)

blocks.text:
What to notice: in old Java, `Person`'s constructor calling the overridden `describe()` saw `officeId == null`, because the subclass field was assigned only after `super(...)` returned. The new rule lets `Employee` initialise `officeId` first, so the overridden method sees the real value. It is a fix for a classic trap (calling overridable methods from constructors, covered in Part 3), but the better advice remains: do not call overridable methods from constructors at all. The fail-fast validation before `super(...)` is the more common use. Record canonical constructors still cannot call `this(...)` or `super(...)` explicitly.

### Scoped values (JEP 506)

Frameworks need to carry context through many layers of calls: the current user, a request id, a transaction. Passing it as a parameter through every method is noisy. The traditional answer is `ThreadLocal`, but it has three problems: it is mutable (any code can `set`), it lives until you `remove` it (or the thread ends, which in a thread pool may never happen, a classic leak), and child threads inherit a *copy*, which is costly when you have millions of virtual threads.

A **scoped value** is the better tool for sharing *immutable* data downward through a call chain. A value is **bound** for exactly the duration of a call (`run` or `call`); inside it, every callee in the same thread, however deep, can `get()` it; when the call returns, the binding disappears automatically. There is no `set` and nothing to remove. A nested `where(...).run(...)` can *rebind* the same value for its own callees; the outer value reappears afterwards.

Scoped values were previews in Java 21 to 24 and are final in 25. The version below uses the same API shape and ran on Java 21 with `--enable-preview`. On 25 you omit the flag.

blocks.title: Sv.java (preview on 21; final in 25)

blocks.code:
$ java --enable-preview --source 21 Sv.java
Note: Sv.java uses preview features of Java SE 21.
Note: Recompile with -Xlint:preview for details.
user=unbound
user=alice
user=bob
user=alice
user=unbound
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text: The output tells the story: unbound outside, `alice` inside, `bob` during the nested call, `alice` again when it returns, and unbound at the end. Without the explicit `isBound()` check, `get()` on an unbound value throws an exception. Scoped values also work with structured concurrency: threads forked inside a `StructuredTaskScope` (still a preview API in 25, the fifth preview, JEP 505) inherit the binding without copying. Ordinary thread pools do not inherit bindings. `ThreadLocal` is not obsolete: it remains right for per-thread caches (a non-thread-safe formatter object per thread) and for mutable per-thread state.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring and other frameworks store request context (security principal, MDC logging fields, tracing ids) in `ThreadLocal`. With virtual threads this still works, but migrating such context to scoped values is a topic for framework authors. As an application developer, remember the pooled-thread leak: always clean up a `ThreadLocal` in a `finally` block.

### Compact object headers (JEP 519)

Every object in the heap begins with a header holding GC and locking information and a pointer to its class (Part 9 shows the layout). Shrinking that header saves memory on every one of millions of objects, which also means fewer cache misses and less GC work. Compact object headers, an experimental feature in Java 24, are a **product feature** in Java 25 but **opt-in**:

blocks.code: $ java -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders -jar app.jar
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
Oracle's JEP reports, on the benchmarks they ran, about 22% less heap and 8% less CPU time on one SPECjbb2015 configuration, 15% fewer collections on another, and about 10% less time for a highly parallel JSON parser. Treat these as upper-end examples, not promises: your gains depend on how many small objects you allocate. The JEP also notes that the layout was used in hundreds of Amazon production services. Because it is not the default in 25, enable it deliberately and measure with your real workload. This flag does not exist on Java 21 (the JVM prints `Unrecognized VM` `option`). Java 27 makes it the default; see the next chapter.

### Faster startup: the AOT cache story (JEP 514, JEP 515)

A JVM starts cold: it loads and links classes, interprets bytecode, and only after profiling does the JIT produce fast code. For short-lived services, serverless functions and CLI tools this warm-up is the cost. Project Leyden's answer is the **AOT** **cache**: record what a typical run of your application loads and links, store it in a file, and reuse it on the next start.

Java 24 (JEP 483) introduced the cache with a two-step workflow (record, then create). Java 25 made it ergonomic (JEP 514): one command creates the cache, and production starts use it.

blocks.code:
$ java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App
$ java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App
blocks.title: Creating and using an AOT cache (Java 25; not run on 21)

blocks.text:
The first command runs a *training run* of your application, and when it exits the JVM writes `app.aot`. The second uses the cache. Use a realistic training run (exercise the code paths that matter) and run production on the same JDK and classpath that created the cache; the cache is tied to them. JEP 515 additionally lets the cache carry method profiles collected during training, so the JIT can reach optimised code sooner after startup. Per the JEP, you can keep the older two-step approach (`-XX:AOTMode=record`, then `-XX:AOTMode=create`) when you train on a small machine and build the cache elsewhere.

The idea is not new on 21. Application class-data sharing (AppCDS) has been available since Java 13 and gives a part of the benefit. This is a real run on 21:

blocks.code:
$ java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp . App
504500
$ java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp . App
504500
blocks.title: AppCDS dynamic archive on Java 21 (the application is a 12-line toy; no timing claimed)

blocks.text: The AOT cache extends this by caching loaded and linked state and, with JEP 515, profiling data. The sizes of the wins depend on how many classes your application loads; Spring Boot applications with thousands of classes see the most benefit.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: An AOT or CDS archive is not portable across JDK versions or vendors, and a changed classpath makes the JVM ignore it (sometimes with only a warning). Build the cache in the same pipeline stage and image as the one that runs the service, not on your laptop.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is new in Java 25 that a backend developer should know? Scoped values (final) as a safer alternative to `ThreadLocal` for immutable context; flexible constructor bodies for validating before `super(...)`; compact source files and instance `main` (and module imports) that simplify scripts and teaching; compact object headers (opt-in, less heap) and easier AOT cache creation for faster startup. Also that structured concurrency, stable values and primitive patterns are still in preview in 25.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Java 25 (Sept 2025) is the current LTS: JEPs 506, 511, 512, 513 and 519 are final or product features.
- Compact source files, instance `main`, `IO.println` and module imports cut ceremony for scripts and teaching.
- Flexible constructor bodies allow validation and field assignment before `super(...)`, without touching `this`.
- Scoped values give immutable, automatically scoped context; `ThreadLocal` remains for per-thread caches.
- Compact headers are opt-in in 25; AOT caches are created with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` and used with `-XX:AOTCache`.

sections.title: Java 26, Java 27 and the road ahead

blocks.text:
Two releases have shipped since Java 25 LTS: Java 26 in March 2026 and Java 27 on 15 September 2026. Neither is an LTS, so most production systems will not run them, but they show where the platform is heading and several changes will reach everyone through the next LTS (expected September 2027). Only items confirmed against the OpenJDK release lists are described here.

### Java 26 (March 2026)

rows: Prepare to Make Final Mean Final
Mutating a `final` field via deep reflection (`setAccessible`) will be warned about now and refused in the future
AOT Object Caching with Any GC
The AOT cache can be used with any garbage collector, not only one
Less synchronisation between application threads and G1, improving throughput
Read and write PEM text for keys and certificates
Values computed on first use, then treated as constants
SIMD API still incubating; waits for Valhalla
blocks.caption: Java 26 JEPs worth knowing.

blocks.text:
Two of these deserve a closer look.

**Final means final (JEP 500).** A `final` field is supposed to be immutable, and the JIT and the memory model assume so. Yet reflection with `setAccessible(true)` can overwrite a final instance field. Serialization libraries and some mocking tools rely on this. JEP 500 makes the JDK warn on such mutation now, as the first step to disallowing it by default, and the JVM can be told how strict to be (check the JEP for the exact option name before you use it). If your tests or frameworks mutate finals, expect warnings after upgrading. The rule of thumb is unchanged: write immutable classes properly (records, final fields) and do not depend on reflection to change them.

**HTTP/3 (JEP 517).** HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP) instead of TCP, which avoids head-of-line blocking between streams and speeds up connection setup. The client from Part 5 gets support for it; you opt in when you build the client by asking for the HTTP/3 version, and the client can fall back when the server does not support it. As with HTTP/2, your application code (`client.send(request, handler)`) does not change.

### Java 27 (15 September 2026)

rows: G1 as the default GC everywhere
No more silent fall back to Serial on small machines
Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3
TLS can combine classical and post-quantum key exchange
The smaller header (from Java 25) is on without a flag
Sensitive values can be removed from recordings
blocks.caption: Java 27 JEPs worth knowing.

blocks.text:
**G1 everywhere (JEP 523).** Since Java 9 the JVM picks G1 on "server-class" machines and Serial otherwise (fewer than 2 CPUs or under about 1.8 GB). Containers with small limits therefore ran Serial without anyone asking. From 27, G1 is chosen regardless of processor count and heap size, because G1 has improved enough to match Serial's throughput and footprint at all sizes. If you run tiny containers and want the old behaviour, name the collector yourself with `-XX:+UseSerialGC`; an explicit choice always wins. Check GC logs and memory (`-Xlog:gc*`) after upgrading small services.

**Compact headers by default (JEP 534).** What was opt-in in 25 becomes the default. The usual reason to care is a library or tool that assumes the old header layout, such as agents or off-heap code that computes object sizes. Check that your tooling supports it, and use the flag in the negative form (`-XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders`) as an escape hatch if it does not.

**Lazy constants (JEP 526/531).** Formerly "stable values" (JEP 502, preview in 25). The use case: a field you want to initialise lazily (a logger, a heavyweight object, a lookup table) but that the JIT should still treat as a constant once set, which `final` plus lazy initialisation could not give you. It is a preview; the API changed between previews and I am deliberately not showing code for it. Read the current JEP before using it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Features that have been preview for several releases (structured concurrency in 25, 26 and 27; primitive patterns; the Vector API) are not abandoned. They are waiting either for feedback or for other projects. Use previews to learn, not in production.

### The road ahead: the big projects

The next years of Java are driven by a handful of long-running OpenJDK projects. They are described here at the level of intent; consult openjdk.org/projects for each one's current state, because the details move.

rows: Smaller, more expressive language: `var`, records, sealed types, pattern matching, text blocks, simple `main`. Delivered through the releases in this Part and still adding pattern features.
Cheap concurrency: virtual threads (final in 21), `synchronized` without pinning (24), scoped values (25). Structured concurrency is still in preview.
Safe, fast access to native code and memory: the Foreign Function and Memory API (final in 22), the Vector API (incubating), replacing JNI.

Value classes: objects without identity that the JVM can lay out flat in memory, plus eventually generics over primitives. It is a long-running effort; the Vector API and some compact-header decisions are linked to it.
Faster startup and warm-up through ahead-of-time work: class-data sharing, AOT cache (24, 25, 26), method profiles.
Smaller object headers; delivered as compact object headers (25, default in 27).
blocks.caption: Major OpenJDK projects.

blocks.text:
The pattern behind these projects is consistent: add the capability as a preview or incubator, gather feedback for a few releases, finalise, and keep compatibility. Code written for Java 8 still runs on Java 27 in nearly all cases. The costs of upgrading are mostly in the surrounding ecosystem: removed APIs, stronger encapsulation, agents and bytecode libraries that need new versions.

### An upgrade checklist, with real commands

Most upgrade pain comes from three sources: new APIs used by mistake, internals that are now locked, and libraries that are too old. Each has a cheap early warning.

1. **1. Compile against the target release, not just the target syntax.** `javac -source 17` still lets you call APIs from

the JDK you are compiling with. `--release` also restricts the API to what the target version has. On the build machine (JDK 21) a call to `List.reversed()` (new in 21) is rejected when targeting 17:

blocks.code:
$ javac --release 17 Rel.java
Rel.java:2: error: cannot find symbol
... System.out.println(l.reversed()); } }
                        ^
  symbol:   method reversed()
  location: variable l of type ArrayList<Integer>
1 error
$ javac --release 21 Rel.java && java Rel
[2, 1]
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
1. **2. Strong encapsulation.** Since Java 16 (JEP 396) and finally in 17 (JEP 403), reflection cannot open non-public

members of JDK classes unless the module opens them. Libraries from the Java 8 era that poke at `String.value` or `sun.misc` internals fail on first use:

blocks.code:
$ java Priv.java
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.reflect.InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field
private final byte[] java.lang.String.value accessible: module java.base does not "opens
java.lang" to unnamed module @3e77a1ed
$ java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED Priv.java
[B@12405818
blocks.title: Terminal

blocks.text:
(The hash after `@` and after `[B@` varies between runs.) `--add-opens` is a stop-gap flag: it lets the old library run while you wait for a fixed version. Find the offenders before the upgrade with `jdeps --jdk-internals app.jar`, which lists the uses of internal JDK APIs and often suggests the supported replacement.

1. **3. Removed and changed things.** Between 8 and 25 some pieces were removed from the JDK: the Java EE and

CORBA modules in 11 (`javax.xml.bind` now needs a dependency), Nashorn in 15, the applet API in 26, and the Security Manager is permanently disabled since 24. The default charset became UTF-8 in 18, which can change how a program reads files that were written with the platform charset. A GC flag you tuned on Java 8 may no longer exist; the JVM prints a warning, or in some cases refuses to start, for unknown options.

1. **4. Run with the new JVM in a staging environment** and compare behaviour under load, not just whether the unit

tests pass. Watch for changes in GC choice (see JEP 523 above), memory and startup.

### Which Java should you choose?

- **New production project:** Java 25 LTS (or 21 if your platform, framework or vendor does not support 25 yet). Check the framework's compatibility matrix first; Spring Boot, for instance, supports particular Java baselines per release.
- **Existing Java 8 or 11 system:** plan a stepped upgrade to 17 then 21 or 25. Expect work around removed modules (`javax.xml.bind`, Nashorn), strong encapsulation (`--add-opens`), and library upgrades. Run tests on each step.
- **Experimenting:** the newest release (27) to try upcoming features, never as the production base.
- **Always:** use a vendor build that receives security updates (Temurin, Corretto, Oracle JDK, Red Hat, Azul and others) and update to the latest patch of your LTS every quarter.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Interviewers like candidates who can say why a team stays on an LTS and what they would check before moving: dependency support, GC and memory behaviour under load, startup, removed APIs, and a rollback plan.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you decide whether to upgrade a service from Java 17 to 25? Check that the framework and all libraries and agents support 25; compile with `--release 25` and run the full test suite; look for warnings about reflection on final fields and illegal access; compare GC logs, memory (try compact headers) and latency under a realistic load test; then roll out gradually with a quick rollback. Benefits to name: virtual threads and sequenced collections from 21, scoped values and flexible constructors in 25, and lower memory and faster startup options.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Java 26 (March 2026) and 27 (September 2026) are non-LTS; important items: final-means-final warnings, HTTP/3, G1 everywhere, compact headers by default.
- Previews and incubators (structured concurrency, lazy constants, primitive patterns, Vector API) are being refined across releases; do not ship them.
- Amber, Loom, Panama, Valhalla, Leyden and Lilliput are the projects shaping the platform.
- Choose an LTS with a supported vendor build, check framework support, and upgrade step by step with tests and a rollback plan.
#### From Java 8 to 25: what changed

items.question: Which releases are LTS releases between 8 and 25?
items.answer: 11, 17, 21 and 25 (plus 8 itself).

items.question: What does this print on Java 21? `var l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));` `System.out.println(l.reversed().getFirst());`
items.answer: `3`. `reversed()` returns a reversed view, and the first element of the view is the last of the original.

items.question: What is the difference between a preview feature and an incubator module?
items.answer: A preview feature is part of the language or core API but disabled unless `--enable-preview`; an incubator module is a separate API module (such as the Vector API) that is not yet part of the standard. Both may change before they become final.

items.question: Why is `case null` useful, and what happened in a pre-21 `switch` on a null value?
items.answer: It handles null inside the switch instead of requiring a separate check. Before 21 a `switch` on a null reference threw `NullPointerException`.

items.question: What is wrong with this code? `record User(String name) { void setName(String n) { this.name = n; } }`
items.answer: Record fields are `final`; assigning `this.name` in a method does not compile. A record is immutable, so there is no setter.

blocks.text: #### Build tools: Maven and Gradle

items.question: What do the GAV coordinates stand for?
items.answer: groupId, artifactId, version: the unique identity of an artifact.

items.question: You run `mvn package`. Which earlier phases run, and which later ones do not?
items.answer: validate, compile, test run before `package` (and others in between); `verify`, `install`, `deploy` do not run.

items.question: A library is needed to compile but the application server supplies it at runtime. Which scope?
items.answer: `provided` (Gradle: `compileOnly`).

items.question: Two dependencies pull in `lib 1.0` and `lib 2.0`. Which version does Maven choose, by default, and how do you override it?
items.answer: The nearest one in the dependency tree (first declared on a tie). Override it with `dependencyManagement` or an exclusion, and confirm with `mvn dependency:tree`.

items.question: Why commit `mvnw` or `gradlew` to the repository?
items.answer: So everyone, including CI, builds with the same tool version without installing it.

blocks.text: #### Testing Java code

items.question: Why does JUnit create a new instance of the test class for every test method?
items.answer: To isolate tests: state from one cannot leak into another, so test order does not matter.

items.question: What is wrong with this assertion order, and why does it matter? `assertEquals(account.balance(), 75L);`
items.answer: Expected must come first. The failure message says "expected: \<actual value\> but was: \<75\>", which misleads you when debugging.

items.question: Why is a test that calls `LocalDate.now()` and compares it to a hard-coded date a bad test, and what is the fix?
items.answer: It depends on the real clock, so it passes today and fails tomorrow. Inject a `Clock` (fixed in tests) and use `LocalDate.now(clock)`.

items.question: In `MiniTest`, what exit status does the program return, and who benefits?
items.answer: 1 when any test failed (0 otherwise); the build server uses the status to fail the pipeline.

items.question: When is `@SpringBootTest` the wrong tool?
items.answer: For logic that needs no Spring: a plain unit test is much faster. Use it for integration of wiring only.

blocks.text: #### Packaging and running Java applications

items.question: What does the `Main-Class` manifest entry do?
items.answer: It names the class whose `main` method `java -jar` runs.

items.question: What is the difference between `jlink` and `jpackage`?
items.answer: `jlink` builds a trimmed Java runtime image from selected modules; `jpackage` wraps an application plus runtime into a native installer for one operating system.

items.question: Why is a multi-stage Dockerfile preferred?
items.answer: The final image contains only a JRE and the jar, so it is smaller and exposes fewer tools; build tools stay in the first stage.

items.question: A container has 2 GB of memory and you run `java -jar app.jar` with default flags. About how large can the heap grow?
items.answer: About 25% by default, roughly 512 MB.

items.question: What is wrong with `ENTRYPOINT java -jar app.jar` (shell form) for graceful shutdown?
items.answer: The shell becomes process 1 and may not forward `SIGTERM` to `java`, so shutdown hooks may not run; use the exec form.

blocks.text: #### Java 25 LTS highlights in depth

items.question: Which `main` signature does Java 25's launcher try first, and which last?
items.answer: First `static void main(String[] args)`; last an instance `void main()` (static before instance, with arguments before without).

items.question: What does `import module java.base;` import, and what ambiguity can appear with `java.sql`?
items.answer: All public top-level types in the packages exported by the module. `java.util.Date` and `java.sql.Date` clash by simple name; add an explicit single-type import.

items.question: What is wrong with this code in Java 21? `Child(int x) { if (x < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException();` `super(x); }` What changes in Java 25?
items.answer: It does not compile: `super(...)` must be first. Java 25 (JEP 513) allows validation statements in the prologue as long as they do not use `this`.

items.question: List two weaknesses of `ThreadLocal` that scoped values fix.
items.answer: Mutable at any time, must be removed manually (leaks in pools), and inherited copies are expensive for child threads. Scoped values are immutable, bound for a bounded scope and not copied.

items.question: How do you turn on compact object headers in Java 25, and what is the default?
items.answer: `-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders`; it is off by default in 25.

blocks.text: #### Java 26, Java 27 and the road ahead

items.question: What changes about the default garbage collector in Java 27, and how do you keep the old behaviour for a tiny container?
items.answer: G1 becomes the default in all environments (JEP 523); Serial was previously chosen on small machines. Keep Serial with `-XX:+UseSerialGC`.

items.question: A library you use changes a `final` field with reflection. What do you expect after upgrading to Java 26?
items.answer: A warning (the first step toward refusing such mutation, JEP 500); check the JEP for the strictness option.

items.question: Which of these are still preview in Java 27: structured concurrency, compact object headers, primitive patterns?
items.answer: Structured concurrency (7th preview) and primitive patterns (5th preview). Compact object headers are on by default in 27.

items.question: Which OpenJDK project delivered virtual threads, and which delivered the Foreign Function and Memory API?
items.answer: Loom and Panama.

items.question: Is Java 26 an LTS release? Which is the next LTS after 25?
items.answer: No; the LTS releases are 8, 11, 17, 21, 25. The next after 25 is expected two years later, in September 2027.
